before_1453: Capital of the shrinking Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire, reduced by 1453 to little more than the city itself and parts of the Peloponnese.
after_1453_short_term: City under Ottoman military administration immediately after 29 May 1453.
after_1453_longer_term: Formal Ottoman capital from 1459 (Necipoglu, citing Kritoboulos) through to 1922-23; the seat of the Ottoman court and government for over four and a half centuries.

before_1453: Hagia Sophia functioned as the Patriarchal cathedral of Orthodox Christianity; multiple churches and monasteries across the city.
after_1453_short_term: Hagia Sophia converted into the city's premier imperial mosque in 1453, keeping its name; the Orthodox patriarchate continued under a new patriarch appointed 6 January 1454.
after_1453_longer_term: Endowments (waqfs) established for major converted and newly built religious complexes (e.g. the 1457 Hagia Sophia waqf and the Fatih complex).

before_1453: Roughly 40,000-50,000 residents at the time of the siege (Schneider's estimate), far below the city's medieval peak.
after_1453_short_term: Population initially fell further; Oz notes an early 1453 wave of Anatolian settlers had returned home by autumn, showing depopulation was not solved by a single transfer.
after_1453_longer_term: Household census of 1477 records 16,324 households on the Istanbul side (~50,000-70,000 people on a conventional multiplier); population climbed further across the following centuries, reaching roughly 15.75 million in the province by end-2025.

before_1453: Byzantine imperial and ecclesiastical bureaucracy centered on the city.
after_1453_short_term: First post-conquest survey (partial) completed in 1455, covering Istanbul and Galata by household.
after_1453_longer_term: Sustained Ottoman administrative apparatus, including household/tax registers such as the 1477 census.

before_1453: Byzantine-era walls, palaces (e.g. Blachernae), churches including the Church of the Holy Apostles, largely in a state of long-term decline and partial disrepair by the 15th century.
after_1453_short_term: Existing fortifications maintained and adapted (e.g. Yedikule Fortress built behind the Golden Gate in 1458).
after_1453_longer_term: New Ottoman palace (Topkapi, 1459-1478) and mosque complex (Fatih, foundation inscription 1463-70, built on the site of the Church of the Holy Apostles) added to the cityscape.

before_1453: Constrained trade, in part due to the city's reduced political and territorial base in its final Byzantine decades (general characterization, low confidence; not independently quantified in the sources reviewed for this project).
after_1453_short_term: Commercial life disrupted immediately by the conquest and by population loss.
after_1453_longer_term: Endowed commercial establishments (shops) attached to major religious complexes from the 1470s (Medium confidence); renewed diplomatic and trade ties with Venice from the 1479 peace treaty (High confidence).

before_1453: City occupied much of the area within the Theodosian walls, though travelers' accounts (cited in period historiography) describe large open or depopulated spaces by the mid-15th century.
after_1453_short_term: Initial post-conquest years included forced and incentivized resettlement programmes to repopulate specific quarters.
after_1453_longer_term: Long-term growth extended the city well beyond the historic peninsula across subsequent centuries, a process this dataset does not attempt to map in detail beyond the population figures in population_context.csv.

before_1453: Walls and the Golden Horn chain served as the primary active defence of a sovereign capital under existential threat.
after_1453_short_term: Rumelihisari and Anadolu Hisari lost most of their strategic purpose once the city itself was in Ottoman hands, since the two fortresses had been built specifically to interdict traffic to a hostile capital.
after_1453_longer_term: The city's fortifications became heritage rather than active defence works over subsequent centuries; the Theodosian walls and related sites were inscribed as part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 1985.
